# Test Setup and Evaluation

## Evaluation Framework

Because no ground truth labels are available, evaluation relies on internal validation
metrics, bootstrap stability, and interpretability rather than external criteria.

### Internal Validation Metrics

Three internal criteria are used to assess cluster quality across all methods. The
**average silhouette width** [@kaufman1990finding] measures how similar each observation
is to its own cluster relative to the nearest competing cluster, with higher values
indicating stronger separation and better-defined structure. The
**Calinski--Harabasz (CH) index** measures the ratio of between-cluster to
within-cluster scatter, where larger values indicate more compact and well-separated
clusters. For the probabilistic methods (PD and FPDC), a **probability silhouette** is
additionally computed using `Silh()` from the `FPDclustering` package
[@tortora2024fpdclustering], which extends the silhouette concept to soft membership
weights and is better suited to evaluating solutions where observations belong
partially to multiple clusters. For k-means only, **total within-cluster sum of squares
(WSS)** is also reported as it directly reflects the k-means objective and is used in
the elbow method for cluster count selection. Because WSS decreases monotonically with $k$, the elbow plot was treated as a method-specific diagnostic rather than a standalone decision rule; when the elbow was weak or ambiguous, silhouette width, the Calinski--Harabasz index, and bootstrap stability were used to finalize the selected value of $k$.


### Stability

Clustering algorithms such as k-means and RKM are sensitive to initialization and local
optima, so a method that yields highly variable solutions across repeated runs may be
unreliable even if its internal metrics appear strong in a single run
[@everitt2011cluster]. Bootstrap stability is therefore assessed for each method by
resampling 30% of users across 15 replicates and comparing each replicate's partition
to the full-data reference solution using the adjusted Rand index (ARI)
[@kaufman1990finding]. ARI ranges from 0 (no agreement beyond chance) to 1 (perfect
agreement), with higher values indicating more reproducible clustering solutions. For PD
and FPDC, hard labels are obtained by assigning each user to their highest-probability
cluster before computing ARI, enabling direct comparison across all four methods on a
common scale.

### Implementation Summary


```{r tbl-tuning-summary, echo=FALSE}
#| tbl-cap: "Tuning ranges and model-selection criteria for each clustering method."

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(knitr)

tuning_summary <- tribble(
  ~Method,               ~`k range`, ~`q range`, ~`nu range`, ~`Primary criterion`, ~`Secondary criterion`, ~`Tertiary criterion`,
  "K-means",             "2-20",     "N/A",      "N/A",       "WSS elbow diagnostic", "Silhouette",           "CH, bootstrap stability",
  "Reduced K-means",     "2-10",     "2-6",      "N/A",       "Silhouette over (k, q)", "CH",                 "Bootstrap stability",
  "PD clustering",       "2-5",      "N/A",      "N/A",       "Probability silhouette", "Silhouette",         "CH",
  "FPDC",                "2-8",      "2-5",      "2, 6, 10",  "Probability silhouette over (k, q, nu)", "Silhouette, CH", "Bootstrap stability"
)

knitr::kable(
  tuning_summary,
  booktabs = TRUE
)
```

All methods were applied to standardized embedding matrices of dimensions 64, 128, and 256. For K-means, WSS elbow plots were used as a method-specific tuning diagnostic, and the final value of $k$ was determined using silhouette width, the Calinski--Harabasz index, and bootstrap stability when the elbow was weak or ambiguous. For Reduced K-means, $k$ and the reduced dimension $q$ were selected jointly over a two-dimensional grid using silhouette as the primary criterion and CH as a secondary check. For the probabilistic methods, model selection emphasized probability silhouette because PD clustering and FPDC produce soft cluster memberships. Accordingly, PD models were selected over $k$ using probability silhouette as the primary criterion, with ordinary silhouette and CH used as supporting diagnostics, while FPDC models were selected over $(k, q, \nu)$ using the same hierarchy. Intermediate results were cached to R Data Serialization or `.rds` files to support reproducibility without rerunning the full pipeline during rendering. The tuning ranges and selection criteria for each method are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:tbl-tuning-summary).
